etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English obstinate, obstinat, from Latin obstinātus, past participle of obstinō (“set one's mind firmly upon, resolve”), from ob (“before”) + *stinare, from stare (“to stand”). Doublet of ostinato.

definitions.definition: Stubbornly adhering to an opinion, purpose, or course, usually with implied unreasonableness; persistent.

quote.citation: 1686, Montaigne, translated by Charles Cotton, That men are justly punished for being obstinate in the defence of a fort that is not in reason to be defended:
quote.text: From this consideration it is that we have derived the custom, in times of war, to punish  […]  those who are obstinate to defend a place that by the rules of war is not tenable  […]

quote.citation: 1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 21, in Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  the junior Osborne was quite as obstinate as the senior: when he wanted a thing, quite as firm in his resolution to get it; and quite as violent when angered, as his father in his most stern moments

definitions.definition: (of inanimate things) Not easily subdued or removed.

quote.citation: 1925-29, Mahadev Desai (translator), M.K. Gandhi, The Story of My Experiments with Truth, Part IV, Chapter XXIX,
quote.text: Now it happened that Kasturbai  […]  had again begun getting haemorrhage, and the malady seemed to be obstinate.

definitions.definition: (of a facial feature) Typical of an obstinate person; fixed and unmoving.

quote.citation: 1925 July – 1926 May, A[rthur] Conan Doyle, “(please specify the chapter number)”, in The Land of Mist (eBook no. 0601351h.html), Australia: Project Gutenberg Australia, published April 2019:
quote.text: He had the same pile of curly hair, but he was clean-shaven with a heavy, obstinate jowl.
